title: Getting Specified Early: How Suppliers Can Influence Projects Before the RFQ Stage
summary: Learn how construction suppliers can influence projects before the RFQ stage by building design relationships, improving product data, and getting specified early.
body_text: By the time an RFQ lands in a supplier's inbox, most of the decisions that actually determine who wins the job have already been made. The spec has been written, the basis-of-design product has often already been chosen, and the supplier responding to the RFQ is frequently bidding against a product that was selected weeks or months earlier — sometimes with little realistic chance of changing that outcome no matter how competitive the price. Suppliers who consistently win more work tend to recognize this earlier than their competitors do: the real competition for most projects doesn't happen at RFQ stage. It happens during design, when the spec is still being written and the basis-of-design decision hasn't been locked in yet. Getting specified early means showing up in that window, instead of arriving after it's already closed. Why RFQ-Stage Competition Is Usually the Wrong Fight Once a spec names a specific product or a tightly defined set of "or equal" criteria written around one product's specifications, every other supplier responding to that RFQ is fighting an uphill battle. They're not really competing on the merits of their product — they're competing to be accepted as an acceptable substitute for a product the design team already chose. That's a much harder position to win from, and it usually means competing primarily on price, because differentiation on performance or features doesn't matter much once the design team already has their preferred option in mind. This is the structural reason a lot of suppliers feel like they're constantly racing to the bottom on price: they're entering the competition at the one stage where price is almost the only lever left to pull. What "Getting Specified" Actually Requires Getting specified early means building a relationship with the people who write specs and influence basis-of-design decisions — architects, engineers, and in many cases the developer's own technical team — well before a specific project's RFQ is ever issued. This isn't about a single sales call. It's about consistent visibility with the people who make these decisions, built through technical resources that make their job easier (clear submittal packages, code-compliance documentation, performance data formatted the way a spec writer actually needs it), and through a track record on past projects that gives a design team confidence in naming a product without having competitively bid it first. Suppliers who do this well tend to think of design teams as a long-term audience, not a one-time sales target. The architect or engineer who specifies a product on one project is very likely to specify it again on the next one, if the product performed well and the supplier was easy to work with — which means the relationship-building investment pays off well beyond a single job. Where This Connects to a Broader Route-to-Market Strategy Getting specified early is one piece of a larger pattern in how suppliers consistently get into projects rather than winning them sporadically. The case for building a consistent route to market rests heavily on this idea — that suppliers who rely entirely on responding to RFQs as they appear are playing a much harder, more reactive game than suppliers who've built relationships upstream of the RFQ stage. Getting specified early is, in many ways, the clearest practical expression of that broader strategy. It Also Changes Who You're Selling To Suppliers focused only on RFQ response tend to sell almost exclusively to GCs and subcontractors, because that's who issues most RFQs. But the people who actually make basis-of-design decisions are frequently on the developer's or design team's side, not the GC's. This is closely related to the shift covered in selling to developers, not just GCs — getting specified early often means building relationships with exactly the audience that post identifies, because developers and their design teams are typically the ones with the authority to name a product in the spec, well before a GC ever issues a competitive RFQ. What This Looks Like in Practice A supplier pursuing this strategy seriously will typically invest in a few concrete things: submittal and spec-language documentation that a design team can drop directly into their own documents with minimal editing, a process for tracking which architects and engineers are working on upcoming projects in a given market, and a way of staying visible with those design teams between projects — not just showing up when there's an active bid to chase. This is also where consistency matters more than intensity. A single well-timed presentation to a design firm rarely changes much on its own. A supplier who shows up reliably, with useful technical resources, across multiple projects over time, is the one who eventually gets named in a spec without having to win a competitive bid for it. From a Single Spec to Repeat Business Getting specified once on a project is valuable on its own, but the bigger payoff comes when that relationship turns into being specified again on the next project, and the one after that. That's really a question of turning a single project into a long-term, repeat customer relationship — getting specified early is how that relationship usually starts, but it isn't the same thing as the ongoing work of maintaining it once it exists. Why This Matters More as Margins Tighten In a market where RFQ-stage competition increasingly comes down to price, getting specified early is one of the few remaining ways for a supplier to compete on something other than the lowest number. A product that's already named in the spec doesn't need to win a price war against an "or equal" substitute — it's the baseline everyone else is being measured against. That's a fundamentally stronger position, and it's available to any supplier willing to invest in the relationships and documentation that make it possible. Merlin Merchant helps suppliers track which projects are moving through design, which design teams they have existing relationships with, and where the basis-of-design decision is still open — so outreach happens during the window when it can actually influence the spec, rather than after the RFQ has already gone out. This kind of structured visibility is also what makes building multiple buildings the same way actually achievable at scale." About Merlin AI Merlin is the operational intelligence and execution orchestration platform built for the construction industry — continuously aligning materials, labour, cost, and decisions in real time across every active project. The platform serves three participants in the construction ecosystem: contractors industrialising through prefab, self-perform, and warehouse operations; developers who need their supply chain to coordinate like a production system; and suppliers looking for a direct route into live construction projects. Merlin EOS runs production operations, Merlin PI coordinates projects, and Merlin Merchant connects suppliers to work. Unlike tools that report on work after the fact, Merlin orchestrates it while it is happening. When Merlin runs production, execution becomes inevitable. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What does "getting specified" mean for a building product supplier? It means a supplier's product is named as the basis-of-design — or as one of a tightly defined set of acceptable products — in the project spec, before the RFQ stage. This gives the supplier a significant structural advantage over competitors responding to the same RFQ. 2. How early should a supplier start building relationships with design teams? As early as possible relative to a project's design phase — ideally well before a specific project even exists, through ongoing relationship-building with architects and engineers who are likely to design projects the supplier wants to be specified into. 3. Is getting specified early only relevant for large suppliers? No. Smaller suppliers can compete effectively in this space because it's driven by relationships and technical resources rather than by the size of the sales team. A supplier with strong, well-documented technical resources can build design-team relationships regardless of company size. 4. How does getting specified early affect price competition? A product that's already named in the spec is the baseline against which substitutes are measured, rather than one of several options competing primarily on price. This generally reduces price pressure compared to responding to an open RFQ. 5. Does getting specified into one project guarantee future work with that design team? Not automatically, but it significantly improves the odds. Design teams that have had a good experience with a product and supplier on one project are considerably more likely to specify the same product again, provided the relationship is maintained between projects.

title: Alexander Zverev won his first Grand Slam title. Choose your own reaction
summary: “If I lost this final, I maybe would have never won a Slam,” he said after beating Flavio Cobolli in five sets.
body_text: © 2026 Ian MacNicol Alexander Zverev needed help. He would find it in the most unexpected way imaginable. Twice he had led by a set against Flavio Cobolli in the Roland Garros final, and twice he had given that lead back. Just a few minutes earlier, he’d been within a couple of points of victory, only to see the younger and lower-ranked Italian snatch it from his jaws, 7-5 in a fourth-set tiebreaker. Now, for the third time in his career, the 29-year-old German was entering the fifth set of a Grand Slam final. He had lost the other two. Was he about to do it again, and squander a chance to win his first major title without having to face Carlos Alcaraz, Jannik Sinner, or Novak Djokovic? At that moment, Zverev said he felt something he hadn’t felt in a decade. A cramp. Normally this would have been the worst development possible, a potential death knell for his chances. Instead, he welcomed the distraction from his own rising inner tension. Read more: Alexander Zverev battles past Flavio Cobolli for first Grand Slam title of career at Roland Garros View this post on Instagram “What kind of helped me, I was cramping a little bit, because I was emotional,” Zverev said. “I haven’t cramped in probably 10 years. I was very nervous, very kind of tightened up, and then, once I cramped, I relaxed, and that helped me.” “I feel like I played better in the fifth set, I played more free, I played more aggressive.” You could see that new freedom in every part of his game. After watching his double fault numbers build in the fourth set, Zverev came out and made 14 straight first serves in the fifth. He broke Cobolli for 0-2 with a nice drop shot that led to a winning pass. Most crucially, he saved two break points at 3-0, the second of them with an outstanding all-court defensive effort that led to a missed Cobolli overhead. This court had some of my best memories, and also some of my biggest heartbreaks. Alexander Zverev about Court Philippe-Chatrier From there, coming down the stretch, when he might have been expected to tense up even more, Zverev didn’t put a foot wrong. When Cobolli’s last smash went awry, he fell to the court, a Slam champ at last. He had been in nearly the same position, in nearly the same spot, under much different circumstances, four years earlier. In the semifinals here against Rafael Nadal in 2022, playing perhaps the match of his life, Zverev had tripped and torn ligaments in his right ankle, an injury that ended his season. View this post on Instagram “This court had some of my best memories, and also some of my biggest heartbreaks,” Zverev said of Chatrier. “Laying on the floor, with seven broken ligaments and two fractured bones.” Zverev knew as well as anyone that, with Alcaraz and Sinner absent, it was essentially now or never for him to put all of his bad memories behind him and rewrite his story. “If I lost this final, I maybe would have never won a Slam,” he said. “Now that I’ve won this, it changes. I feel like I’ve done it. Maybe I can enjoy these finals a bit more, play my best tennis.” Normally, a breakthrough win at a major is cause for celebration around the sport. The reaction to Zverev’s triumph is bound to be more mixed. View this post on Instagram There are reasons, if you choose, to respect his achievement and his career. He’s a player who has many friendships among his colleagues, who doesn’t engage in gamesmanship on the court, who plays with juvenile diabetes, who has endured several crushing late-round defeats but kept going, and who survived the pressure of being the favorite over the past week. There are also reasons, if you choose, not to laud his victory. He has been accused by two women of domestic abuse. In one case, an ATP investigation ended with no disciplinary action, due to “insufficient evidence.” The other case was settled out of court in Germany; Zverev paid a 200,000-euro settlement fine, without admitting guilt. He denies both allegations. I don’t dismiss or ignore anything about Zverev, neither the good nor the allegedly bad. Watching the match today, my main thought was that it would have been fun to see Cobolli’s reaction to winning. Now that the match is finished, I’m glad the final was a good one, Zverev's quest is behind us, the tournament is over, and a whole new season starts tomorrow.

title: Template-Based vs Template-Free OCR: What’s the Real Difference?
summary: Template-free OCR uses AI and LLMs to automatically recognize data from any document layout, unlike template-based approaches that rely on rigid rules.
body_text: The difference between template-based and template-free OCR comes down to how reliant each one is on template to read documents. Template-based OCR provides automated data extraction that’s bound to a fixed field mapping, making it ideal for standardized, repetitive documents. Template-free OCR, on the other hand, offers more flexible data extraction that can adapt to any layout without additional configuration, perfect for handling varying, unpredictable document formats. Which one should you use? There’s no one-size-fits-all answer on which one is the best. The right OCR model depends on your document volume, how often vendors or formats change, and how much setup time you’re willing to invest upfront. TL;DR: Key Differences At a Glance Criteria Template-Based OCR Template-Free OCR How it works Matches documents to a predefined layout with fixed field positions Uses ML/LLMs to interpret structure and context dynamically Setup time Faster for narrow, consistent use cases Slower initially, no per-format setup needed afterward Accuracy High, as long as the document matches the template Generally high, but can dip on unusual or low-quality layouts Flexibility Low. Breaks when layout changes High. Adapts to new or unfamiliar layouts Scalability Limited. Each new format needs a new template Strong. Scales easily across vendors and formats Maintenance Growing overhead as templates pile up Minimal ongoing maintenance once deployed Cost Lower long-term cost for repetitive, high-volume formats Higher upfront cost; often cheaper via ready-made solutions Compliance/auditability Easier to explain and audit (fixed logic) Harder to explain (model-based reasoning) Best for Standardized, repetitive documents from few sources Diverse, unpredictable documents from many sources Template-Based OCR Pros: High accuracy on matching layouts: The system already knows exactly where each field sits, so there’s little potential for misreading or misinterpretation. Cost-efficient at scale for repetitive formats : Once the template is built, the system simply applies the same logic repeatedly, meaning no ongoing model training required. Easier compliance auditing: Because field positions are fixed, it’s simple to document and justify why a specific value was extracted, which matters in regulated industries like finance or healthcare. Cons: Rigid to layout changes: Even a small shift, like a vendor updating their invoice format or design, can drastically break extraction accuracy. Growing maintenance overhead: Every new document variant means building and managing another template, which can add more turnaround time and maintenance cost. Limited scalability: Keeping up with hundreds of formats becomes harder to maintain as document volume grows. When to use: If your organization deals with standardized, repetitive documents from a limited number of sources, such as customer registration forms, sales order forms, or invoices from one or two regular vendors. Template-Free OCR Pros: Adapts to varying layouts : Leverages ML and LLMs to identify fields based on context rather than fixed position, so it can read a document correctly even if the layout has never been seen before. Scales easily across vendors : Processing documents from new vendors becomes frictionless as the system can instantly interpret unfamiliar layouts without needing to be retrained first. Handles edge cases efficiently : It performs reliably with the real complexity of business documents where formats, field placement, and structure vary. Cons: Higher implementation cost : Building an advanced OCR system in-house demands significant computational power and training data, which is why many businesses opt for ready-to-use AI OCR solutions instead. Inconsistent results without predefined rules : Extraction relies on contextual understanding, not fixed logic, so results can vary across batches. Setting a specific rule on what data to extract beforehand is highly recommended for this model. When to use: If your organization routinely processes documents from many different vendors, especially when those formats are frequently changing, such as accounts payable departments handling invoices from hundreds of suppliers. How Each One Actually Work s Both approaches start the same way: document upload. Once the document is detected by the system, this is where the extraction process differs. Template-based OCR matches the document against the template it was built for that defines exactly where each field is placed. For example, “invoice number” always in the top-right corner, “total amount” always in the bottom table. The OCR engine scans only those fixed coordinates and maps the text directly to its field, delivering clean data as a result. Template-free OCR uses advanced AI and LLM models to intelligently interpret any document structure that comes in. It reads context, such as labels, surrounding text, and visual patterns, to figure out what each piece of data represents. It can recognize that a number following “Total” is likely the total amount, no matter where it appears on the page. The resulting data is accurately structured, regardless of layout. How to Evaluate Which One Is Right for Your Business Choosing between these two OCR data extraction models takes careful consideration of several factors, such as document structure consistency, processing volume, implementation budget, and scalability needs. Here’s a step by step guide to help you find the better fit for your business document process. 1. Assess Your Document Types Start by reviewing the documents you process most often. If they follow a consistent format, template-based OCR may be sufficient. If layouts vary across vendors, customers, or regions, template-free OCR is often a better fit. 2. Evaluate Document Volume Consider how many documents you process each month. Higher volumes generally benefit from solutions that minimize manual setup and maintenance. 3. Consider Maintenance Requirements Think beyond implementation. Template-based OCR requires ongoing template creation and updates, while template-free OCR typically requires less maintenance. 4. Align with Future Growth Choose a solution that can scale with your business, support new document types, and adapt to evolving workflows. As you expand into new markets, onboard new vendors, or launch new products, your document formats are likely to multiply and diversify. 5. Test with Your Actual Documents Before committing, run a test using your own documents, ideally a mix of your most common and most variable formats, to see how each option performs in practice. This hands-on step often reveals fit issues that aren’t obvious on paper, helping you make a more confident, informed decision. People Also Asked How does template-free OCR differ from template-based OCR? Template-based OCR relies on predefined document layouts and requires a new template whenever a format changes. Template-free OCR uses AI to understand document structure and context, enabling seamless extraction of data from varying layouts without per-template creation. Is template-free OCR more expensive to implement than template-based OCR? While implementation costs vary by provider and use case, template-free OCR can prove to be more cost-efficient in the long term by eliminating the need to create, maintain, and update document templates. This can be especially valuable for organizations processing documents from multiple vendors, customers, or regions. What is the best strategy for migrating from template-based to template-free OCR? A phased migration is usually the most effective approach. Start with document types that have the highest volume or the most layout variations, adopt template-free OCR alongside existing workflows, validate the results, and gradually expand adoption. This minimizes disruption while ensuring extraction quality meets business requirements. What document types are best suited for template-based OCR and template-free OCR? Template-based OCR works best for standardized documents with consistent layouts, such as fixed-format forms, applications, invoices from a single vendor, and internal business documents. Template-free OCR is better for processing documents that come from multiple sources.

title: Heat Treatment of Metals: Processes, Types, and Purpose
summary: Turbocharge the way you order custom parts with our instant quoting engine. Get DFM feedback, lead times, and pricing in a matter of clicks, not days.
body_text: Heat treatment of metals refers to a set of controlled thermal processes that alter the physical and mechanical properties of metals through precise heating and cooling cycles. Heat treatment of metals plays a foundational role in modern manufacturing, where achieving the right balance of hardness, strength, ductility, and wear resistance determines the performance and longevity of a finished part. Industries ranging from aerospace to automotive rely on the process to produce components that meet strict mechanical and dimensional standards. Heat treating encompasses a broad range of techniques, each designed to target specific material behaviors at the microstructural level. Processes (annealing, normalizing, quenching, and tempering) address different engineering needs, from softening metals for easier machining to hardening surfaces for wear resistance. The methods apply to ferrous and select non-ferrous metals, making the process adaptable across material types. Heat treatment is a critical step that defines how a part performs under real-world mechanical loads in precision manufacturing environments. Xometry supports a wide range of heat treatment services, providing manufacturers with access to properly processed metals that meet design and performance specifications. Understanding heat treatment of metals helps engineers make informed decisions about material selection and processing. What Is Heat Treatment? Heat treatment is a controlled thermal process that involves heating a metal to a specific temperature, holding it at that temperature for a set duration, then cooling it at a predetermined rate to alter its physical and mechanical properties. The process does not reshape or remove material from the part. Instead, it modifies the internal microstructure of the metal, producing changes in hardness, strength, toughness, ductility, and wear resistance. Heating temperatures vary widely depending on the metal and intended outcome, ranging from approximately 150°C (302°F) for low-temperature tempering to above 900°C (1,652°F) for high-temperature annealing of steel. Cooling rates are equally variable, from slow furnace cooling in annealing to rapid quenching in water or oil for hardening. The combination of temperature, hold time, and cooling rate determines the final microstructural state of the metal. Engineers apply the process to raw stock, semi-finished parts, or finished components, depending on the manufacturing sequence. Applications span tooling, structural components, fasteners, gears, and precision-machined parts across industries where mechanical performance is non-negotiable. Why Is Heat Treatment Important in Manufacturing? Heat treatment is important in manufacturing because it directly controls the mechanical properties that determine how a part performs under load, friction, and stress. Raw metal as delivered from a mill may not meet the hardness, strength, or ductility requirements of a finished component. Heat treating bridges the gap from raw material to performance-ready part without altering geometry or dimensions. Hardness improvements from quenching and tempering allow steel components to resist surface wear, extending service life in high-friction environments like gears and cutting tools. Annealed metals exhibit improved machinability, reducing tool wear and cutting forces during CNC operations, which lowers production costs. Stress relief treatments prevent distortion and cracking in welded or heavily machined parts by eliminating residual internal stresses built up during prior processing. Normalized metals achieve a uniform grain structure that improves predictability in mechanical testing and quality control. In industries where part failure carries safety consequences (aerospace, automotive, and medical devices), heat treatment is not optional but a mandatory process step governed by engineering specifications and material standards. Does Heat Treatment Change the Chemical Composition of Metals? No, though thermochemical processes like carburizing and nitriding do change the chemical composition of the surface layer. The process operates entirely on the internal microstructure, rearranging atoms within the existing crystal lattice through controlled heating and cooling without introducing or removing alloying elements. The metal retains the same elemental makeup it had before treatment. What changes is the arrangement, size, and phase of the grains within the material. Steel subjected to quenching transforms austenite into martensite, a harder crystalline phase, yet the carbon and iron content remain identical. The separation of chemistry from structure is what makes heat treatment especially valuable in precision manufacturing. Engineers achieve dramatically different mechanical behaviors from the same alloy by varying only the thermal cycle applied. Part geometry is also preserved throughout the process, meaning a heat-treated component maintains its dimensional form while gaining improved performance characteristics. The ability to improve performance without altering part geometry is the basis for understanding the broader category of metal properties, which outlines how the composition of metals relates to processing and application decisions. What Is the Purpose of Heat Treatment? The purposes of heat treatment are listed below. Hardness Improvement : Heating and rapid cooling, as in quenching, produce hard microstructures like martensite in steel, increasing surface and bulk hardness to resist wear and indentation. Steel hardness values achievable through quenching range from 55 to 68 HRC, depending on alloy composition and carbon content. Strength Enhancement : Controlled thermal cycles refine grain structure and modify phase distribution, raising tensile and yield strength in the treated metal. Precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys (7075-T6) reach tensile strengths exceeding 570 MPa through aging treatment. Ductility and Toughness Recovery : Annealing restores ductility in work-hardened metals, enabling further forming or machining operations without cracking. Softened metals exhibit elongation values 10% to 20% higher than their hardened counterparts. Stress Relief : Residual stresses from welding, casting, or heavy machining are reduced through low-temperature heat treatment, preventing distortion and cracking during service. Machinability Improvement : Softening through annealing or normalizing reduces cutting resistance, extends tool life, and improves surface finish quality in machined components. Wear Resistance : Case hardening processes (carburizing and nitriding) produce a hard outer surface while preserving a tough interior, extending part life in abrasive or high-contact applications. How Does Heat Treatment Improve Mechanical Properties? Heat treatment improves mechanical properties by altering the microstructure of the metal at the grain and phase level through precise thermal cycles. When a metal is heated above its critical transformation temperature, its atoms gain enough energy to rearrange into a new crystalline phase. The rate at which the metal cools from that point determines which phase forms and in what proportion. Rapid cooling produces hard, fine-grained structures like martensite, while slow cooling yields softer, coarser phases like pearlite or ferrite. Each microstructural state corresponds to a distinct set of mechanical properties. Tempering a quenched steel part at temperatures from 150°C to 650°C adjusts the balance from extreme hardness with high brittleness toward a tougher, more impact-resistant state. Grain refinement through normalizing increases yield strength by restricting dislocation movement within the crystal lattice, a mechanism described by the Hall-Petch relationship, where strength increases as grain size decreases. The ability to tune these outcomes by adjusting temperature, hold time, and cooling rate gives engineers direct control over the mechanical profile of the finished part. Can Heat Treatment Increase Metal Strength Without Changing Shape? Yes, heat treatment increases metal strength by modifying the internal microstructure while leaving part geometry unchanged. The thermal process operates at the atomic level, altering grain size, phase distribution, and crystalline structure without adding, removing, or repositioning material. A steel shaft treated by quenching and tempering achieves tensile strengths from 800 MPa to over 2,000 MPa, depending on the alloy and thermal cycle, all while retaining its original diameter and length within standard dimensional tolerances. The independence of strength gain from geometry change is particularly valuable in precision-engineered components, where tight tolerances are established during machining and must be preserved through subsequent processing. Minor dimensional changes from thermal expansion are predictable and accounted for in process design. Parts destined for high-load applications in tooling, dies, and structural assemblies undergo heat treatment after machining to reach final mechanical specifications. The process is foundational in CNC Machining, where CNC machining workflows incorporate heat treatment as a planned step to deliver components with both dimensional accuracy and the required mechanical performance. What Are the Types of Heat Treatment Processes? The types of heat treatment processes are listed below. Annealing : A softening process that heats the metal above its upper critical transformation temperature, holds it, then cools it slowly to relieve stress and improve ductility. Normalizing : A grain-refining process for carbon and low-alloy steels that heats metal above its critical temperature and allows air cooling to produce a uniform, stronger microstructure than annealing. Hardening (Quenching) : A rapid cooling process from elevated temperature that produces hard phases like martensite, significantly increasing surface and bulk hardness. Tempering : A post-quench process that reheats the metal to a controlled lower temperature to reduce brittleness while retaining improved hardness. Case Hardening (Carburizing and Nitriding) : A surface treatment that introduces carbon or nitrogen into the outer metal layer, hardening the case while preserving a tough interior core. Aging (Precipitation Hardening) : A controlled heating process used on specific alloys to precipitate hardening particles within the matrix, increasing strength over a defined time and temperature cycle. Annealing Annealing is a heat treatment process in which a metal is heated to a temperature above its recrystallization point, held for a sufficient time, then cooled slowly, typically inside the furnace, to soften the material, relieve internal stresses, and restore ductility. The process reverses the hardening effects of cold working or prior thermal cycles by allowing grains to recrystallize into a new, strain-free structure. Steel annealing temperatures range from 750°C to 900°C (1,382°F to 1,652°F), depending on the grade, while the hold time at temperature varies from 1 hour to several hours based on part cross-section. Cooling rates in furnace annealing are kept below 20°C per hour to ensure the formation of soft phases like ferrite and pearlite. The result is a metal with improved machinability, reduced hardness, and higher elongation values that make it suitable for forming, drawing, or further machining operations, which describes how annealing applies across steel, copper, and aluminum alloys. Normalizing Normalizing is a heat treatment process in which a metal is heated above its upper critical temperature, then removed from the furnace and cooled in still air at room temperature. Air cooling is faster than furnace cooling, producing a finer grain structure and higher strength compared to annealed metal, while still achieving better uniformity than untreated material. Steel normalizing temperatures fall in the range of 830°C to 950°C (1,526°F to 1,742°F), depending on carbon content and alloy composition. The refined grain structure produced by normalizing improves impact toughness, fatigue resistance, and dimensional consistency across the cross-section of the part. Normalized steel also exhibits improved machinability relative to as-rolled or as-cast material because the microstructure is more uniform and predictable. The process is applied to castings, forgings, and rolled products before final machining to ensure consistent mechanical behavior, which details how normalizing achieves grain refinement and property enhancement across different steel grades. Hardening (Quenching) Hardening, performed through quenching, is a heat treatment process in which metal is heated to its austenitizing temperature and then rapidly cooled in a quenching medium (water, oil, polymer solution, or air) to lock in hard microstructures. In steel, rapid cooling suppresses the formation of soft phases and forces the crystal structure into martensite, a body-centered tetragonal phase that is significantly harder than pearlite or ferrite. Steel hardness after quenching reaches 60 to 68 HRC, depending on the carbon content and alloy composition, with higher carbon levels generally producing harder martensite. The quenching medium determines the cooling rate: water quenching produces the fastest cooling and highest hardness but carries greater distortion and cracking risk, while oil quenching offers a slower, more controlled rate suited to alloy steels. Air-hardening steels (H13 and D2 tool steel) achieve adequate hardness through air cooling alone due to their high alloy content, which suppresses transformation during slower cooling. Quenched parts are typically brittle immediately after treatment, which is why hardening is almost always followed by tempering to restore toughness. Tempering Tempering is a heat treatment process applied after quench hardening in which the metal is reheated to a temperature below its lower critical point, held for a defined time, then cooled to reduce brittleness and internal stress while preserving a useful level of hardness. Quenched steel without tempering is extremely hard but too brittle for most structural and tooling applications. Tempering temperatures range from 150°C to 700°C (302°F to 1,292°F), avoiding the 200°C to 420°C (400°F to 800°F) range, with lower temperatures preserving high hardness for cutting tools and higher temperatures producing tougher, more impact-resistant parts for structural use. At 200°C, tempered steel retains hardness near 60 HRC, while tempering at 600°C reduces hardness to approximately 30 to 40 HRC but significantly improves impact toughness. The transformation during tempering involves the decomposition of martensite into tempered martensite, with the precipitation of fine carbide particles that stabilize the structure. The combination of a high-hardness quench followed by controlled tempering is referred to as quench-and-temper treatment, which is among the most widely applied thermal processes for structural steel, tool steel, and machine components. Case Hardening (Carburizing and Nitriding) Case hardening is a heat treatment method that selectively hardens the outer surface layer of a metal part while preserving a softer, tougher core beneath. The process targets wear resistance at the contact surface without reducing the impact toughness of the underlying material, making it suited for gears, shafts, camshafts, and bearing races that experience simultaneous surface wear and bulk mechanical loading. Carburizing introduces carbon into the surface of low-carbon steel by heating the part in a carbon-rich atmosphere at temperatures from 850°C to 1,050°C (1,562°F to 1,922°F), allowing carbon to diffuse into the outer layer to a depth of 0.5 mm to 2.5 mm before quenching. The carbon-enriched case transforms to hard martensite upon quenching, reaching surface hardness values of 58 to 63 HRC. Nitriding introduces nitrogen into the metal surface at lower temperatures, from 480°C to 580°C (896°F to 1,076°F), without requiring a subsequent quench, reducing distortion risk. Nitrided surfaces reach hardness from 65 to 72 HRC in suitable alloy steels and exhibit excellent fatigue resistance due to compressive surface stresses introduced by the nitriding reaction. Aging (Precipitation Hardening) Aging, referred to as precipitation hardening, is a heat treatment process applied to specific alloy systems in which a supersaturated solid solution is held at a controlled elevated temperature for a defined period, causing fine particles of a second phase to precipitate within the metal matrix and impede dislocation movement. The process applies primarily to aluminum alloys (2000, 6000, and 7000 series), nickel superalloys, and stainless steels (17-4 PH). The treatment sequence begins with a solution heat treatment that dissolves alloying elements into a single-phase solid solution at high temperature, followed by rapid quenching to retain the supersaturated state, then aging at a lower temperature to precipitate strengthening particles. Artificial aging temperatures for aluminum alloys range from 115°C to 190°C (239°F to 374°F), with aging times from 6 to 24 hours depending on the alloy and temper designation. Natural aging occurs at room temperature over days to weeks in certain aluminum alloys (2024-T3). The strengthening mechanism relies on precipitates blocking dislocation movement, with peak strength achieved at the point of maximum precipitate density before overaging causes particle coarsening and strength reduction. How Does Heat Treating Work on a Microstructural Level? Heat treating works at the microstructural level by supplying thermal energy to a metal's atomic lattice, enabling phase transformations, grain recrystallization, and diffusion of alloying elements that redefine the material's mechanical behavior. At room temperature, metals exist in stable crystalline phases with defined grain sizes and dislocation densities accumulated from prior processing. When heated above specific critical temperatures, the crystal structure transforms into a higher-energy phase. In steel, heating above the A3 temperature (typically 750°C to 912°C depending on carbon content) converts the room-temperature body-centered cubic (BCC) ferrite into face-centered cubic (FCC) austenite, which holds carbon in solid solution more readily. The subsequent cooling rate determines which low-temperature phase forms from the austenite. Slow cooling produces lamellar pearlite or soft ferrite. Rapid quenching forces the structure into hard martensite. Intermediate cooling rates generate bainite, a structure with a toughness-hardness balance between pearlite and martensite. Diffusion-based processes (carburizing and nitriding) operate by driving atoms of carbon or nitrogen from the surrounding atmosphere into the metal surface through thermally activated diffusion, enriching the surface layer without changing the core chemistry. Every measurable mechanical property, from hardness to fatigue limit, traces directly to the microstructural state produced by the thermal cycle. What Changes Occur in Metal Grain Structure? Grain structure in metals undergoes distinct changes during heat treatment depending on the temperature applied and the cooling rate used. At temperatures below the recrystallization threshold, individual grains remain largely intact, though residual stresses are partially relieved through a process called recovery, where dislocations rearrange within grains without forming new grain boundaries. Above the recrystallization temperature, existing deformed grains dissolve, and new, strain-free grains nucleate and grow, replacing the prior structure entirely. The size of the newly recrystallized grains depends on temperature and hold time. Higher temperatures and longer times produce larger grains, while shorter cycles at lower temperatures generate finer grains. Grain growth beyond the optimal range reduces strength and toughness, a condition called overheating or grain coarsening. In steel, the transformation from ferrite to austenite on heating involves a complete change in crystal structure from BCC to FCC, and the reverse transformation on cooling produces different grain structures depending on cooling rate. Martensite formed by rapid quenching is characterized by fine, needle-like (acicular) grains with high internal stress, contributing directly to its extreme hardness. Normalized structures display equiaxed, medium-sized grains with a uniform distribution of phases. Does Grain Structure Control Metal Strength? Yes, grain size and structure directly control the strength, hardness, and ductility of a metal. The relationship between grain size and yield strength follows the Hall-Petch equation, which states that yield strength increases as grain diameter decreases. Smaller grains present more grain boundaries per unit volume, and grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation movement, the primary mechanism of plastic deformation. A fine-grained normalized steel achieves yield strengths 15% to 30% higher than the same steel in a coarse-grained annealed condition. Martensite, with its extremely fine acicular grain structure and high dislocation density, delivers the highest hardness achievable in steel through heat treatment. Coarse-grained metals, by contrast, offer lower strength but improved ductility, as dislocations travel greater distances before encountering boundaries. Grain shape matters alongside size: equiaxed grains produced by recrystallization behave isotropically, while elongated grains from rolling or forging create directional strength differences. Grain structure refinement through normalizing or controlled quenching is a primary tool for increasing strength and durability in precision components, making it fundamental to process selection in demanding applications. What Metals Can Be Heat Treated? The metals that can be heat-treated are listed below. Carbon and Alloy Steels : The most widely heat-treated metals, capable of hardening through quenching, strengthening through normalizing, and softening through annealing across the full range of carbon contents from 0.2% to 1.4%. Tool Steels : High-alloy steels (H13, D2, M2, and A2) engineered for heat treatability, reaching hardness values from 40 to 68 HRC after quenching and tempering. Stainless Steels : Martensitic grades (410 and 440C) respond to hardening treatments, while precipitation-hardening grades (17-4 PH) gain strength through aging cycles. Aluminum Alloys : Heat-treatable grades (2024, 6061, and 7075) respond to solution treatment and aging, reaching tensile strengths from 270 MPa to over 570 MPa. Titanium Alloys : Alpha-beta alloys (Ti-6Al-4V) respond to solution treatment and aging, achieving tensile strengths above 1,100 MPa. Nickel Superalloys : Alloys (Inconel 718 and Waspaloy) gain strength through precipitation hardening, retaining mechanical properties at elevated service temperatures above 700°C. Copper Alloys : Certain grades (beryllium copper) respond to precipitation hardening, reaching tensile strengths from 1,000 MPa to 1,400 MPa after aging treatment. Can Steel Be Heat Treated? Yes, steel can be heat-treated. Steel is the most widely heat-treated metal in industrial manufacturing, with a broad range of heat treatment processes applicable to nearly every steel grade. The carbon content and alloying elements in steel determine the degree to which thermal treatment alters mechanical properties. Low-carbon steels (0.05% to 0.25% carbon) respond well to case hardening through carburizing, which enriches the surface layer with carbon before quenching. Medium-carbon steels (0.3% to 0.6% carbon) are the primary candidates for through-hardening by quenching and tempering, achieving tensile strengths from 700 MPa to 1,200 MPa. High-carbon steels (0.6% to 1.4% carbon) reach the highest hardness values after quenching, making them suited for cutting tools, springs, and wear-resistant components. Alloy steels (4140, 4340, and 8620) incorporate chromium, molybdenum, and nickel to improve hardenability, allowing larger cross-sections to achieve uniform hardness throughout. Stainless steels respond differently depending on grade: martensitic grades harden through quenching, while austenitic grades (304 and 316) are not hardenable by heat treatment but respond to stress relief and solution annealing, which addresses how steel grades respond to different thermal processing cycles. Can Aluminum Alloys Be Heat Treated? Aluminum alloys are heat-treatable within a defined subset of the alloy family, specifically those designated as heat-treatable grades by their ability to form a supersaturated solid solution. Non-heat-treatable aluminum alloys (1000, 3000, and 5000 series) gain strength only through cold working and cannot be precipitation hardened. Heat-treatable grades (2000, 6000, and 7000 series) respond to solution heat treatment followed by quenching and aging. The 6061 alloy in the T6 temper achieves a tensile strength of approximately 310 MPa after artificial aging, compared to 125 MPa in the fully annealed condition. The 7075-T6 alloy reaches tensile strength above 570 MPa, making it one of the strongest commercially available aluminum alloys. Solution treatment temperatures for aluminum range from 460°C to 540°C (860°F to 1,004°F) depending on alloy chemistry. Quenching is performed in water to retain the supersaturated solution before aging causes precipitation. Overaging, a condition where aging time or temperature exceeds the optimum, reduces strength due to precipitate coarsening and is deliberately applied in the T73 temper for improved stress corrosion resistance at the cost of some strength, which details how aluminum alloy selection affects heat treatment response and final mechanical properties. Are All Metals Suitable for Heat Treatment? No, not all metals respond to heat treatment in ways that produce useful mechanical property changes. The suitability of a metal for heat treatment depends on whether its crystal structure undergoes a phase transformation or precipitation reaction at achievable temperatures. Pure aluminum, pure copper, and commercially pure titanium do not respond to precipitation hardening because they lack the necessary alloying elements to form strengthening precipitates. Austenitic stainless steels (304 and 316) cannot be hardened by quenching because their face-centered cubic structure does not transform to martensite on cooling. Wrought iron and gray cast iron have limited heat treatment responses due to their high carbon content in graphite form. Ferrous metals, particularly carbon and alloy steels, represent the broadest class of heat-treatable metals, with well-documented transformation behavior across a wide range of temperatures and cooling rates. Non-ferrous metals (beryllium copper, aluminum alloys, and titanium alloys) require specialized processes tailored to their specific phase diagrams and diffusion kinetics, unlike the more standardized procedures applied to steel. What Are the Industrial Applications of Heat Treatment? The industrial applications of heat treatment are listed below. Tooling and Die Manufacturing : Tool steels (D2 and H13) are quenched and tempered to hardness levels from 40 to 65 HRC, providing the wear resistance and toughness needed for cutting, stamping, and forming dies operating under high cyclic loads. Automotive Engineering : Gears, crankshafts, camshafts, and axle shafts are carburized or induction-hardened to achieve hard, wear-resistant surfaces with tough cores, withstanding the combined bending, torsional, and contact stresses present in drivetrain applications. Aerospace Components : Titanium alloys, nickel superalloys, and precipitation-hardened steels undergo solution treatment and aging to meet the high strength-to-weight ratio and temperature resistance requirements of turbine blades, structural frames, and fastener systems. CNC Machined Parts : Precision-machined components in aluminum (6061-T6 and 7075-T6) and steel (4140 and 4340) are heat-treated before or after machining to achieve final mechanical specifications while maintaining tight dimensional tolerances. Medical Devices : Surgical instruments and implants in martensitic stainless steel (440C) and titanium alloys are heat-treated to achieve the hardness, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility required for clinical use. Energy and Power Generation : Pressure vessel steels, turbine discs, and valve components are normalized and tempered to achieve toughness and creep resistance under high-temperature, high-pressure service conditions. Uses in Tooling and Die Manufacturing Tooling and die manufacturing represents one of the highest-demand applications for heat treatment because tool steels must simultaneously resist surface wear, retain dimensional stability at elevated temperatures, and absorb impact loads without fracturing. Cold work tool steels (D2, A2, and O1) are hardened by quenching from austenitizing temperatures of 780°C to 1,050°C (1,436°F to 1,922°F) to hardness levels of 60 to 65 HRC, then tempered at temperatures from 150°C to 250°C to reduce brittleness while maintaining cutting edge integrity. Hot work tool steels (H13 and H11) operate at elevated service temperatures and require tempering at 540°C to 650°C (1,004°F to 1,202°F) to resist thermal softening during repeated heating and cooling cycles in die casting and hot forging applications. High-speed steels (M2 and T1) used in cutting tools are triple-tempered at approximately 560°C (1,040°F) to convert retained austenite to martensite and precipitate secondary carbides that provide secondary hardening, reaching a final hardness of 64 to 67 HRC. Dimensional stability after heat treatment is controlled through cryogenic treatment at temperatures as low as -196°C (minus 321°F), which converts retained austenite to martensite and stabilizes the tool steel before final grinding. Uses in Automotive Engineering Automotive engineering applies heat treatment across a broad range of drivetrain, structural, and chassis components where wear resistance, fatigue strength, and toughness operate simultaneously under dynamic loading. Carburized and case-hardened gears in manual and automatic transmissions achieve surface hardness from 58 to 62 HRC with a case depth from 0.8 mm to 1.5 mm, providing contact fatigue resistance over service lives exceeding 200,000 miles. Crankshafts in medium and heavy-duty engines are induction-hardened at the journal surfaces to 50 to 58 HRC, improving wear resistance at bearing contact points while retaining the toughness of the core to absorb cyclic bending and torsional loads. Suspension springs and torsion bars made from medium-carbon alloy steels (5160 and 9260) are quenched and tempered to tensile strengths from 1,400 MPa to 1,800 MPa, then shot peened to induce compressive surface stresses that extend fatigue life. Aluminum components in engine blocks, cylinder heads, and wheels made from 319 and A356 alloys receive T6 heat treatment to achieve the strength and dimensional stability needed for precision bore and mounting surface tolerances. Valve seats and camshaft lobes in engines made from powder metal or cast iron are case-hardened or nitrided to resist the high-temperature wear generated by repeated cam and valve contact cycles. Uses in Aerospace Components Aerospace applications impose the most demanding combined requirements of any heat treatment application, including high strength, low weight, elevated temperature resistance, and fatigue performance that must be maintained over service lives measured in tens of thousands of flight hours. Titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, the most widely used aerospace structural alloy, is solution treated at 900°C to 950°C (1,652°F to 1,742°F) and aged at 480°C to 540°C (896°F to 1,004°F) to achieve tensile strengths above 1,100 MPa at densities roughly 56% lower than steel. Nickel superalloys (Inconel 718 and Waspaloy) used in turbine discs and blades undergo multi-stage heat treatment sequences with solution treatment, rapid quench, and double aging cycles to precipitate gamma-prime and gamma-double-prime strengthening phases, retaining strength at temperatures above 700°C (1,292°F) where most steels would creep or soften. Precipitation-hardened stainless steel (17-4 PH) is used for structural fasteners, fittings, and brackets where corrosion resistance and strength above 1,000 MPa are needed without the weight of alloy steel. Aluminum alloys (7075-T73 and 7050-T7451) applied in aircraft wing skins and structural frames are aged to the T7 overaged condition to resist stress corrosion cracking under sustained tensile loads in humid environments, accepting a moderate strength reduction in exchange for reliability. Uses in CNC Machined Parts CNC-machined parts frequently require heat treatment either before machining to achieve stable, machinable material conditions or after machining to reach final mechanical specifications without distorting the precision geometry established during cutting operations. Pre-machining annealing of tool steels and alloy steels reduces hardness to a machinable range below 30 HRC, enabling efficient stock removal at high cutting speeds with extended tool life. After roughing operations, parts destined for hardening are semi-finished with stock left for finish grinding after heat treatment to account for minor dimensional changes from the thermal cycle. Aluminum components (6061 and 7075) machined to tight tolerances for aerospace or industrial fixtures are supplied in the T6 or T651 condition, meaning solution treatment and aging are performed on the stock before machining, with the final part dimensions cut into already-heat-treated material. Stress relief treatment at 500°C to 650°C (932°F to 1,202°F) is applied to heavily machined steel parts before final finishing to release residual stresses that would cause distortion in service, where understanding the thermal conditioning of CNC machined parts informs machine setup and material selection decisions. How Does Heat Treatment Improve Manufacturing Performance? Heat treatment improves manufacturing performance by delivering parts with mechanical properties that raw material cannot achieve, reducing downstream failure rates, and enabling more aggressive design specifications. A component heat-treated to a precise hardness and strength specification performs predictably under load, which reduces the safety factors engineers must apply in structural calculations and allows lighter, more efficient designs. Improved machinability from annealing or normalizing reduces cutting tool consumption and cycle times in production machining, directly lowering the cost per part. Case-hardened components operating in wear applications last 3 to 10 times longer than untreated parts of the same geometry, reducing replacement frequency and maintenance downtime. Stress-relieved parts maintain dimensional accuracy over time in service, eliminating the gradual distortion that would otherwise cause misalignment, vibration, or premature bearing failure in precision assemblies. Heat treatment enables the use of lower-alloy, lower-cost base materials in applications that would otherwise require expensive high-alloy grades, as thermal processing can raise the performance of a moderate-cost steel to meet demanding specifications. Quality control in heat treatment, verified through hardness testing, microstructural examination, and mechanical testing of witness samples, provides documented proof of conformance that meets aerospace, automotive, and defense industry standards. What Benefits Does Heat Treatment Provide in Engineering Design? The benefits that heat treatment provides in engineering design expand the range of achievable mechanical properties from any given alloy, giving engineers the ability to tailor material performance to meet specific loading, wear, and environmental conditions without changing part geometry or material grade. A single alloy (4140 steel) delivers a yield strength of approximately 415 MPa in the annealed condition, rising to over 1,080 MPa after quenching and tempering at 315°C (599°F), representing a strength gain exceeding 160% through thermal processing alone. The capacity to harden selectively through induction hardening or case hardening allows engineers to apply maximum surface hardness only where wear occurs while maintaining core toughness for impact resistance, a combination that is impossible to achieve through alloying alone. Heat treatment enables the use of thinner cross-sections in structural components, reducing weight while meeting the same load-bearing requirements as a heavier untreated part. Fatigue life improvements from shot peening combined with prior heat treatment extend component service cycles in rotating machinery, reducing unplanned downtime. Dimensional stability in precision tool and die components after heat treatment and stress relief ensures that dies retain their cutting geometry over production runs of hundreds of thousands of parts, maintaining part quality without tool replacement. Can Heat Treatment Reduce Manufacturing Failures? Yes, heat treatment reduces manufacturing failures by addressing the root causes of premature part failure at the microstructural level before components enter service. Fatigue cracking, the most common failure mode in cyclically loaded components, initiates at stress concentrations amplified by residual tensile stresses from machining or forming. Stress relief treatment eliminates the tensile residual stresses that accelerate fatigue crack initiation, extending fatigue life by factors of 2 to 5 in treated components compared to untreated equivalents. Wear failure in gears, bearings, and cam followers is reduced by case hardening, which raises surface hardness to the range required to resist abrasive and adhesive wear mechanisms over the intended service life. Hydrogen embrittlement, a failure mode in high-strength steels subjected to electroplating or acid pickling, is mitigated through low-temperature baking at 190°C to 218°C (375°F to 425°F) starting within 1 to 4 hours of plating, which drives hydrogen from the metal before embrittlement cracking initiates. Dimensional failures from distortion during service are prevented through pre-service stress relief and normalizing, which stabilize the microstructure against further change under operating temperatures. The reduction in failure risk from heat treatment is critical for high-stress mechanical applications (turbine components, landing gear, and engine valves) where part failure carries safety and operational consequences far exceeding the cost of the thermal process.

title: Your service catalog belongs in your incident response.
summary: When an incident hits, context shouldn't be scattered. The Rootly x Cortex integration brings your service catalog into incident response, so every responder works from the same map.
body_text: An incident starts. Before anyone can fix anything, the incident commander has to answer a string of questions to kick off the response work. What service is this? What does it depend on? Who owns it? Has this happened before, and what did we do last time? Is there a runbook, and where does it live? For most teams, the answers are scattered. Some live in a service catalog, some in a wiki, some in the heads of whoever happened to be on call the last time it broke. The commander stitches the picture together by hand while the clock runs. That stitching is dead time, and it happens during the worst possible moment. The teams that respond the fastest do so because they already have their map drawn. Every service, team, dependency, and owner is defined as an entity in a catalog, and that catalog is wired directly into the place where incident response happens. When something breaks, the context is already attached to it. That's where the Rootly x Cortex integration comes in, it brings the business entities you've already modeled in Cortex into Rootly’s native catalog , so your incident response is built on the same source of truth as the rest of your engineering org. Context is the thing responders are short on Speed in an incident is mostly a context problem. The failure itself is often clear with automated probable root cause analysis and similar incident matching doing a lot of heavy lifting upfront. What can be slow is everything around it; figuring out impact radius, finding the owning team, pulling up the right runbook, remembering whether this is a known issue. When your catalog entities live inside Rootly, that work is already done. The affected service has clear owners, Slack channels, its repository, and dependencies. Supercharged with Rootly’s AI Agent, all responders need to do is simply ask for what they need, and the assistant is able to reply with accurate, well-rounded information. Gather similar past incidents impacting the same cluster, or see who was on-call last week for this service to page them for help. This is how knowledge silos break down. The context that used to live with a handful of senior engineers becomes shared across all responders seamlessly. A responder who has never touched this service before gets the same map as the person who built it. That's the difference between an incident that escalates because nobody knows who to call and one that routes to the right team right away. You can't improve reliability you can't measure Long-term reliability comes from learning from your incidents, not just resolving them one at a time. And the quality of what you learn depends on the context you can tie each incident back to. When you have a clear understanding of the business impact behind every incident, the insights you draw across all of them get sharper and more accurate. When incidents are attached to business entities, you can finally measure reliability the way the business actually experiences it. Which services generate the most incidents? Which teams are carrying the heaviest response load? Where is repeat pain concentrated, and what's the real cost of leaving it unaddressed? Without entities, every incident is a one-off. With them, patterns become visible, and patterns are what let you move from reacting to incidents to preventing them. That's the shift from reliability as a cost center to reliability as something you can steer. You can point reliability investment at the services that need it, make the case for that work with data instead of anecdotes, and watch the trend line move. What the integration does Cortex is where many engineering teams already define their entities: services, teams, agents, domains, and the relationships between them. The integration brings those into Rootly’s catalog without asking you to re-model anything. You can connect Cortex and Rootly easily in Rootly’s Integration section of the web app . From there, you can map any Cortex Catalog into Rootly’s catalog. Cortex stays the source of truth . The sync runs on a recurring 24-hour cycle, with an on-demand sync button when you need an update immediately. This allows your commanders and response teams to consistently pull from up-to-date information about your business, and prevents data drift between the two systems. The result is a single pane of glass. The catalog your engineers already maintain becomes the foundation your incident response and reliability reporting are built on, with no parallel system to keep in step. What’s next? Measuring reliability across your business doesn’t stop at incident response. It starts and ends with bringing the right people into the room. Through your Cortex and Rootly integrations, you’ll be able to build on-call processes across your teams and services to ensure you have complete coverage. From there, you’ll be able to see who's on-call for any service or entity and build scorecard rules to enforce on-call coverage standards across your catalog. All directly in Rootly and Cortex, respectively. Get started If you're already on Rootly, you can connect Cortex today. Check out our changelog to learn more, then head to the integrations page in the Rootly web app, map your first Cortex Catalog to a Rootly Catalog, and run a sync. If you're new to Rootly, start a trial and see what incident response looks like when every responder works from the same map.

title: What 25 Years in Energy Has Taught Me About Resilience
summary: Nicole Bulgarino discusses how the concept of energy resilience has evolved over the past 25 years and why it matters more than ever.
body_text: Resilience has been part of the energy sector’s vocabulary for decades. But over the past 25 years working in the industry, and as Co-President of a leading energy infrastructure solutions provider, I’ve seen firsthand how its definition has evolved over time. Early on in my career, resilience was often interchangeable with reliability. Thinking was largely reactive. We identified known failure points, built in redundancy, and planned for the risks we could see coming – the typical disruptions. That approach still applies today, but it also reflects a different, perhaps more predictable, time. Since then, several factors have forced the industry to rethink what resilience really means. Severe weather occurrences, aging infrastructure built 50 to 70 years ago, global volatility, and the rapid advancement of technologies like AI have all played a role in reshaping the concept. Now, resilience is more than just a buzzword, but a practical framework for planning around major, and often unknown, disruptions. Most importantly, these factors have made it increasingly clear that resilience is about people. The energy leaders making challenging decisions, the teams designing our infrastructure, and the communities who depend on it every day are just as critical in resilience planning as the technical components. Understanding resilience from both a technical and human lens is how we best navigate uncertainty. That dual approach is key to a resilient energy future, and the difference between enduring and simply recovering. Designing for Adaptability Throughout the course of my career, the most successful projects I’ve been a part of have all shared one common trait: they were built to perform and adapt. Take Ameresco’s work with the Joint Forces Training Base Los Alamitos , for example. The facility is home to a microgrid that is designed to be resilient, built on a combination of solar power, battery storage, and backup generator capacity. During a particular outage caused by a foil balloon, the microgrid detected the loss of grid power instantly and went into ‘islanded mode’ in seconds. When grid power was restored, it smoothly reconnected without any interruption to operations. This example shows how energy systems can be designed to respond to the environment around them in real time, rather than simply waiting to be fixed. Generally speaking, that design philosophy is more important now than ever. The rapid expansion of AI and data centers is driving electricity demand at a scale our existing grid infrastructure was not built to handle. According to the International Energy Agency, global demand is already outpacing grid upgrades, with investments needing to increase by 50% by 2030 to keep pace. At the same time, that pressure is surfacing real opportunities to modernize infrastructure. AI-optimized facilities require dedicated, behind-the-meter generation deployed on accelerated timelines, infrastructure that performs without adding strain to a grid already under stress. Getting that right is fundamental to both near-term growth and long-term resilience. But the technical solution alone is not enough. It also requires a human foundation, one backed by leadership, coordination, and the ability to make sound decisions when the environment is anything but simple. Understanding the Human Impact of Resilience It’s easy to focus just on the technical terms when considering resilience: redundancy, switching times, and system recovery. And while these concepts are important, reliance ultimately ladders back to the human impact. For critical facilities, power disruptions can have real human consequences. At a hospital, a few seconds matter when it comes to patients getting the care they need. At a water treatment facility or military installation, a few minutes can compromise an entire system and the people depending on it. The margin for error at these facilities is not measured in hours, and the communities they serve cannot afford to treat resilience as an aspiration. I’ve been fortunate enough to work on a number of different projects with a variety of different organizations, from federal agencies to utilities to large institutions. Those who plan for resiliency are protecting more than just infrastructure; they are protecting people and the systems they depend on every single day. And throughout the process, they’re building something a little harder to measure, but no less important: trust. These Systems Also Require Resilient Leadership Today’s energy leaders face a unique set of challenges. Innovation cycles are tightening, policies continue to shift, and sustainability has become less operational and more aspirational. And, as we’ve seen, electricity demand keeps climbing. Balancing near-term performance against decisions that will impact future outcomes in this kind of environment is particularly challenging. This is why investing in collaboration is so important. Ensuring the right people have a seat at the table, including engineers, operators, policymakers, finance teams, and more, helps ensure perspectives are aligned and that we fully understand how each decision will impact the system as a whole. Consistency matters just as much as collaboration. When teams are under pressure, they look for steadiness, especially in an industry constantly inundated by change. Leaders who provide that steadiness in both their words and daily commitments, actions, and values tend to earn a different kind of trust. And that trust has a ripple effect, all the way to the organization’s impact on its community. Looking Ahead The energy landscape will keep evolving. New technologies will emerge and demand adaptation. Infrastructure challenges will continue to shift. What should stay constant is the commitment to planning resilience from the outset, across the systems being built and the people responsible for leading and operating them. The organizations that tend to navigate this best made an intentional choice early on. They recognized that technical resilience and human resilience are connected, and they built specifically around that understanding. The bar will keep rising. But the knowledge, tools, and talent to meet it have never been more within reach. What has Ameresco learned about energy resilience over the past 25 years? Ameresco has learned that energy resilience has evolved from a reactive focus on reliability into a broader framework that includes planning for both known and unknown disruptions. The company emphasizes integrating technical system design with human decision-making to better navigate uncertainty and sustain long-term performance. How does Ameresco define energy resilience in today’s evolving energy landscape? Ameresco defines energy resilience as the ability to anticipate, adapt to, and recover from disruptions. This modern definition reflects challenges such as severe weather, aging infrastructure, global volatility, and rapid technological change, requiring more dynamic and forward-looking planning approaches. What does Nicole Bulgarino say about how resilience has changed in the energy industry? Nicole Bulgarino explains that resilience has expanded beyond reliability and redundancy to include adaptability and preparation for unknown disruptions. She emphasizes that modern resilience depends on both strong infrastructure and the leadership needed to manage increasingly complex and unpredictable operating environments. How does Ameresco design resilient and adaptable energy systems? Ameresco designs energy systems to perform and adapt in real time by integrating technologies such as solar, battery energy storage, and backup generation. This approach enables systems to respond to outages as they occur and supports uninterrupted operations across critical facilities. What does Ameresco’s Los Alamitos microgrid demonstrate about energy resilience? Ameresco’s microgrid at Joint Forces Training Base Los Alamitos demonstrates resilience by instantly detecting a grid outage and transitioning to islanded mode within seconds. The system maintained uninterrupted operations and seamlessly reconnected when grid power returned, showcasing real-time system adaptability. How is rising AI and data center demand shaping Ameresco’s resilience strategy? Ameresco recognizes that AI and data center growth are accelerating electricity demand beyond existing grid capacity. The company is addressing this challenge by developing resilient, behind-the-meter energy infrastructure that performs without adding strain to a grid already under stress. Why does Nicole Bulgarino emphasize the human element in energy resilience? Nicole Bulgarino emphasizes that resilience is about people as much as technology because energy systems support critical services and communities. She highlights that leadership, coordination, and sound decision-making are essential, especially in environments where even brief power disruptions can have serious consequences. What role do leadership and collaboration play in Ameresco’s approach to resilience? Ameresco views leadership and collaboration as essential to resilience because energy decisions span engineering, operations, policy, and finance. By aligning cross-functional teams and maintaining consistency under pressure, Ameresco supports stronger decision-making and more effective, system-wide outcomes. # Originally published on Linkedin #

title: Customer support workflow strategies for scaling startups | Pylon
summary: Learn how to build a repeatable B2B customer support workflow that scales with your startup across all your ticketing systems and Slack, email, and chat.
body_text: Informal customer support is fine for most early-stage startups. Anyone can resolve issues directly in Slack or via email without a formal ticketing system or standardized processes. As the company grows, the informal approach breaks down. Team members lose track of who’s answering what questions between platforms, and response time slows. A well-defined customer support workflow removes bottlenecks and creates simple, clear processes for repeatable operations from customer onboarding to cross-channel follow-ups. In this article, we’ll explore how to create a scalable customer service workflow process that doesn’t add unnecessary complexity. What a customer support workflow looks like for a growing B2B startup Issue view from Pylon A B2B customer support workflow is a standardized process that defines how your support team responds to customer requests. Systems built on a shared email inbox and Slack DMs stop working when there are hundreds of tickets every month and multiple people who route and resolve them. A formal workflow can help you coordinate across ticketing and communication channels as your company grows. Adding omnichannel coordination to a customer support workflow, which collects information from all threads, means structures can evolve with your company and support teams’ needs. Here’s a six-step example of a customer service workflow for a B2B SaaS company: Intake. A customer sends a message describing an error through an existing channel (like email or live chat). Prioritization. The issue is logged in the ticketing system and prioritized based on urgency, business impact, and customer tier. Modern customer support tools often automatically handle this stage with AI. Routing. The ticket is sent to the support team or logged in a support software platform, then assigned to a specific team member. Investigation. There’s often waves of new customers going through the onboarding process as startups grow. Growing startups have complex internal operations with several teams involved in resolving issues for customers. Feed these rules to your AI-powered support platform, and it will handle the process automatically. Automation at this stage makes escalation much more consistent.
